## Introduction

Few inventions have reshaped human civilization as profoundly as the transistor. This tiny semiconductor device, capable of amplifying and switching electronic signals, stands as the foundational building block of modern technology. From smartphones and computers to satellites and medical devices, transistors underpin virtually every electronic system in contemporary life. Understanding the history of the transistor reveals not only a story of scientific discovery but also the interplay of corporate research, wartime necessity, and international competition that defined the twentieth century.

Before the transistor, electronics relied on vacuum tubes—glass-enclosed devices that controlled electron flow in a vacuum. Invented by John Ambrose Fleming in 1904 and improved upon by Lee de Forest with his triode in 1906, vacuum tubes made radio, television, and early computers possible. However, they were fragile, bulky, consumed enormous power, and generated significant heat. ENIAC, one of the first electronic computers completed in 1945, contained roughly 18,000 vacuum tubes, occupied an entire room, and required constant maintenance as tubes burned out regularly.

Scientists had long suspected that solid-state materials might offer an alternative. The phenomenon of rectification—the ability of certain materials to allow current to flow in only one direction—had been observed in crystal detectors used in early radios since the 1870s. Copper oxide and selenium rectifiers were commercialized in the 1920s and 1930s. Yet the theoretical understanding of how electrons behaved within semiconductors remained incomplete, limiting the development of more sophisticated devices.

The decisive breakthrough came at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey. The group included William Shockley, a brilliant and ambitious physicist, along with John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, who joined the effort in the fall of 1945.

Their work built upon the quantum theory of solids, which had matured during the 1930s through the contributions of Felix Bloch, Alan Wilson, and others.     """
    Merge overlapping (or touching) closed intervals.

    Args:

    if not intervals:
        return []

    sorted_intervals = sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: (iv[0], iv[1]))
